See the new trailer below, and some screens too.
Today, Ubisoft announced that Steep Road to the Olympics, an expansion to the open world action-sports game Steep (launched in December 2016) and an Official Licensed Product of the Olympic Winter Games PyeongChang 2018, integrates professional athletes from all around the world into the in-game story mode. Available on December 5, 2017 on PlayStation 4 computer entertainment system (includes enhanced features on PS4 Pro), Xbox One (includes enhanced features on Xbox One X) and Windows PC. Steep Winter Games Edition including Steep base game and Steep Road to the Olympics expansion are now available for pre-order.
In Steep Road to the Olympics story mode, players will experience the journey of a young athlete training in three freestyle events (Big Air, Half Pipe and Slopestyle) to reach the Olympic Winter Games and be the first athlete ever to win gold in 3 freestyle events. The competition takes place in the unique South Korean mountains, where the Olympic Winter Games are being held this coming February. Players will also be able to explore the mountains of Japan, carving through unique powder and exceptional environments.
Before each challenge, players will be treated to training tips and insights from Olympians on the variety of Steep Road to the Olympics events, track designs and the competition itself. Video testimonials from 10 legends and rising stars will be integrated in-game: Lindsey Vonn, American Alpine Skiier who has won numerous competitions including a gold medal in the downhill event at the Olympic Winter Games Vancouver 2010; Kevin Rolland, French freestyle skier and progressive risk taker who won an Olympic bronze medal in the halfpipe at the Olympic Winter Games Sochi 2014; Sage Kotsenburg, American snowboarder who won the first-ever Olympic gold medal in men’s snowboard slopestyle at the Olympic Winter Games Sochi 2014; Ayumu Hirano, Japanese competitive snowboarder who won an Olympic silver medal in the halfpipe at the Olympic Winter Games Sochi 2014; Alexis Pinturault, a French alpine ski racer and Olympic medalist in 2014 for Giant Slalom; Tessa Worley, a French competitor of all five alpine disciplines and specialist of Giant Slalom; the Australian snowboarder Scotty James, a 2x world Halfpipe champion and 2017 Superpipe champion; Gus Kenworthy, an American freestyle skier who won the silver medal in Ski Slopestyle at the Olympic Winter Games Sochi 2014; young American snowboarder and 2017 Slopestyle snowboarding champion, Julia Marino and Bode Miller, an Olympic gold medalist and the most decorated male American alpine ski racer of all time.
The expansion will feature fresh Alpine Skiing, Snowboard and Freestyle Skiing events, including: Giant Slalom, Slalom, Super-G, Downhill, Parallel Giant Slalom, Halfpipe, Snowboard Cross, Slopestyle, Big Air, Ski Halfpipe, Ski Cross and Ski Slopestyle.
The expansion Steep™ Road to the Olympics can be purchased for $30 and Steep™ Winter Games Edition that includes the base game Steep and the expansion can be purchased for $60. Steep Winter Games Gold Edition, with the base game Steep, the expansion, and the Year 1 Season Pass, which gives players access to three previously-released DLC packs featuring additional sports, challenges and outfits will be available for $80.
With development led by Ubisoft Annecy*, Steep – the open world action sports game to feature ski, snowboard, paraglide, wingsuit, rocket wingsuit, sled, base jump and speed riding – designed for a culture that’s all about sharing experiences with the world. Steep features seamless multiplayer, populating the world with players as they explore the Alps and Alaska. Players and friends across the globe can take on challenges together, or compete with each other to snag the top spot on the leaderboards. The game’s replay feature expands this experience, allowing players to relive their wildest tricks and memorable lines and even share them as videos on social media. It doesn’t stop there, as challenges can be created from any line to compete with friends and achieve the best time or score based on customizable factors, such as completing tricks to score. Players can also participate in several competitive live programs such as the monthly Steep World Tour, where players take on specific challenges to qualify in tournaments and have a chance to win exclusive rewards.

User: Can you summarize some strategies recommended by expert travelers to make frequent traveling easier and hassle-free?: Frequent travelers are smart travelers—they know how to make jet-setting easier and hassle-free. Whether it’s knowing how to bypass TSA and customs quicker, battling jet lag or getting a free hotel upgrade, globetrotters know the ins and outs of being on the road and in the air.
After speaking to expert travelers, here are several strategies they recommend that can help other frequent flyers survive this type of lifestyle.
If you’re on a plane several times a year, and you hate waiting in those long lines at customs and/or airport security (where you find yourself packing and unpacking not only your suitcase but also yourself), then we recommend signing up for Global Entry (for those who often fly internationally), and TSA PreCheck.
Global Entry allows you to fly right through customs when you come back into the U.S. Rather than waiting in line, you check yourself in via an automated kiosk. Meanwhile, TSA PreCheck allows you to quickly pass through airport security without having to take anything off or take items out of your bag(s). The cost of signing up for Global Entry is US$100, which is valid for five years (if you have a Platinum AMEX, it’s $0). By signing up for Global Entry, you are automatically eligible for TSA PreCheck, for free.
If you don’t fly internationally often, then you can opt to sign up for TSA PreCheck alone for US$85, which is valid for five years. If you ask us, it’s better to just pay the additional $15 and get both. Because who knows, you may find yourself heading on a few international trips within the next five years, and that extra time saved can make all the difference!
At times, non-stop and direct flights are misunderstood as being one and the same, but they are completely different. A direct flight may still stop, but rather than switching planes like you would on a layover, you would just stay seated on the plane. On the other hand, a non-stop flight doesn’t stop at all until it reaches its final destination. As such, frequent travelers recommend that it’s best to choose non-stop rather than direct to save you time—those extra 2 or maybe even 3 hours of free time will be well worth it!
Traveling often means that soreness and stiffness come hand-in-hand. Sitting for several hours in an airplane seat is not ideal, so to combat tension and possible pain, bring a few tennis balls on the plane with you. Best way to use them is by rolling them under your feet and your thighs to keep stiffness at bay.
Traveling, regardless if it’s across the country or across the world, can take a toll on your mind and body. That’s why it’s important to find the right cure for jet lag—everyone is different and what works for one doesn’t necessarily work for another. For the best tips, check out our blog on How to beat jet lag when traveling domestically or internationally.
When business is slow, the concierge is known to upgrade guests to better rooms for free as long as they ask the front desk politely (and as long as there are not many other people around).
Before asking, double check to make sure that the hotel is, in fact, not full. You can either call and ask beforehand or check online on the hotel’s website to see how many rooms are still available.
If you’re a frequent flyer with tips that you can share with us (and everyone else), please comment below! We would love to hear what secrets you’ve learned while on the road and in the air.
Agent: Expert travelers recommend signing up for Global Entry and TSA PreCheck to bypass long lines at customs and airport security, choosing non-stop flights over direct flights to save time, bringing tennis balls on the plane to combat soreness and stiffness, and finding the right cure for jet lag. They also suggest politely asking the hotel concierge for a free room upgrade during slower business periods, but to double check beforehand to ensure there are available rooms.

User: Can you provide more tips or strategies for dealing with jet lag when traveling internationally?
Agent: Certainly! Here are some additional tips for dealing with jet lag when traveling internationally:

1. Adjust your sleep schedule before you leave: Start adjusting your sleep schedule a few days before you leave so that it aligns with the time zone of your destination. This can help reduce the impact of jet lag once you arrive.

2. Stay hydrated: Dehydration can exacerbate the symptoms of jet lag, so be sure to drink plenty of water before, during, and after your flight.

3. Avoid alcohol and caffeine: Both alcohol and caffeine can disrupt your sleep, making it harder for you to adjust to the new time zone. Try to avoid them on your flight and in the days leading up to your trip.

4. Get some sunlight: Exposure to sunlight can help regulate your body clock and reduce the effects of jet lag. Try to spend some time outdoors during the day, especially in the morning.

5. Take a nap: If you arrive at your destination feeling tired, it can be helpful to take a short nap (no more than 20-30 minutes) to help you feel more alert and refreshed.

6. Use melatonin: Melatonin is a natural hormone that can help regulate your sleep-wake cycle. You can purchase melatonin supplements over-the-counter in most countries. However, you should consult with your doctor before taking them.

7. Give yourself time to adjust: Jet lag can take a few days to fully resolve, so be patient and give yourself time to adjust to the new time zone. Try to avoid scheduling important meetings or activities for the first day or two after you arrive.

Hopefully, these strategies will help you deal with jet lag and enjoy your international travels!

User: Can you provide tips or strategies for getting better sleep on a long-haul flight?
Agent: Definitely! Here are some tips and strategies for getting better sleep on a long-haul flight:

1. Choose the right seat: If you can, choose a window seat so that you can lean against the wall of the plane for support. If you are tall or have long legs, an aisle seat might be more comfortable so that you can stretch your legs.

2. Bring the right gear: Pack a travel pillow, a light blanket or scarf, and noise-canceling headphones to help block out noise and make yourself comfortable.

3. Dress comfortably: Wear loose-fitting, breathable clothing that will not restrict your movement or contribute to discomfort.

4. Stay hydrated: Drink plenty of water before and during the flight and avoid alcohol and caffeinated beverages, as they can disrupt your sleep.

5. Set your watch to your destination time zone: This can help your body adjust to the new time zone and make it easier to fall asleep when you arrive at your destination.

6. Create a restful environment: Use the airline's earplugs and eyeshades if they provide them, or bring your own. You can also use relaxation techniques, such as deep breathing or meditation, to calm your mind and body.

7. Consider natural sleep aids: You may consider using natural sleep aids such as lavender essential oil or valerian root supplements to help you relax and fall asleep.

8. Plan for your arrival: Set an alarm on your phone or request a wake-up call from the flight attendant to ensure that you do not oversleep and miss your connecting flight or arrival time.

By following these tips and strategies, you can get better sleep on a long-haul flight and arrive at your destination feeling rested and refreshed.

User: Can you provide more examples of how airlines use data to personalize pricing for customers?
Agent: Certainly, here are some examples of how airlines use data to personalize pricing for customers:

1. Loyalty program data: Airlines analyze data from loyalty programs to determine which customers are more likely to use their miles to upgrade or purchase additional services.

2. Search history: Airlines track the search history of customers, including the destination, dates, and times of the flights they search for. They may then use this data to offer personalized pricing for future flights to the same location.

3. Location data: Airlines use location data to track where customers are searching from and what offers are relevant to them based on their location.

4. Purchase history: Airlines analyze customers' purchase history to determine which products and services they are most likely to purchase in the future.

5. Device data: Airlines analyze data about the device customers use to book flights and offers tailored promotions based on the type of device being used.

6. Social media data: Airlines may use social media data to determine which customers are more likely to share their travel experiences on social media and offer them promotions and rewards for doing so.

7. Demographic data: Airlines collect demographic data, such as age, gender, and income, to personalize pricing and offers based on the needs and preferences of different customer segments.

Overall, the data gathered and analyzed by airlines is used to create a personalized and seamless booking experience, offering customers the right product at the right price.

1. Demand forecasting: By analyzing past booking patterns and the search trends of customers, airlines can forecast future demand for certain routes, flights and seats. This helps them to price their products accordingly and maximize their revenue opportunities.

2. Dynamic pricing: Through data analysis, airlines can determine the optimal pricing for each flight, taking into account several factors such as demand, competition, cost, and customer behavior. The pricing is adjusted dynamically in real-time to enhance revenue as demand and supply factors fluctuate.

3. Inventory management: Airlines monitor the inventory of all the flights, seats, and products they offer, and adjust the availability and pricing based on demand trends. Analyzing customer segments, such as business travelers or low-fare seekers, helps airlines allocate the available inventory to meet the needs of these customers.

4. Ancillary revenue optimization: Airlines have considerably increased ancillary revenue streams by offering personalized products and services to customers based on their preferences and behavior. Data analytics helps airlines to identify new products and service opportunities, as well as to optimize pricing for existing products.

5. Loyalty Program optimization: Airlines use data analytics to optimize frequent flyer programs by determining which rewards and benefits most appeal to customers. With this information, airlines can incentivize certain behaviors, such as higher value ticket purchases, in exchange for more lucrative rewards, which helps them to boost customer loyalty and revenue over time.

By leveraging such data-driven revenue management practices, airlines can better understand their customers, anticipate their needs, and optimize revenue potential, thus driving lasting growth and profitability.

User: Can you compare and contrast the Toronto International Film Festival with other major film festivals around the world in terms of scope and focus?
Agent: Certainly, here's a comparison of the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) with other major film festivals:

Cannes Film Festival: The Cannes Film Festival is the most prestigious in the world, and showcases some of the most important films from around the world. Unlike TIFF, Cannes is primarily focused on auteur-driven films that showcase strong artistic vision and innovation. Cannes is also distinct from TIFF in that it has stronger connections to the art world, as many of the films that premiere there are considered works of art.

Venice International Film Festival: The Venice International Film Festival is similar to TIFF in that it showcases a mix of American and international films, but it is more European-focused than TIFF. Venice also prizes auteur-driven films, like Cannes, but it is less focused on premieres and more on the overall quality of the films that are shown.
